readings.title: Amabel
readings.challenge: Track how the words just before a repeated name change its meaning from stanza to stanza.
readings.focus: A speaker confronts what time has done to a woman he loved, and to his love.
readings.context: Thomas Hardy (1840–1928), best known for his novels of rural Wessex, his name for southwest England, published his first book of poems, Wessex Poems, in 1898; it gathers verse written over thirty years, some of it in the 1860s. This poem is dated 1865, when Hardy was twenty-five. The speaker meets a woman he loved when they were young. “Custom-straitened” means narrowed by habit and convention; a knell is a funeral bell; “numbers” are verses; a dorp is a village and a dell a small valley; the Last Trump is the trumpet of Judgment Day.

excerpt.locator: Amabel, the whole poem with its date; opens “I MARKED her ruined hues, Her custom-straitened views, And asked, “Can there indwell My…”; closes “1865.”.

questions.prompt: Every stanza ends on the name “Amabel.” How do the words just before it change, from “My Amabel” to “An Amabel”?
facilitatorNotes: The refrain moves from asking whether his Amabel still lives inside the changed woman, through a “knell” and “Spoilt,” to “An Amabel”: any man finds one somewhere. The name stays the same while she becomes, for him, replaceable; then comes the final farewell.
evidence: Can there indwell My Amabel?
All find in dorp or dell An Amabel.

questions.prompt: What changes in Amabel does the speaker notice? Are they all changes of age, or also of character?
facilitatorNotes: Faded colouring, a brown gown once rose, a mechanical step, a spoiled laugh; but “custom-straitened views” describes a mind narrowed by convention. Some readers find the speaker shallow for judging her looks; others think he mourns her lost liveliness. Both can cite these lines.
evidence: Her custom-straitened views
Her step’s mechanic ways Had lost the life of May’s

questions.prompt: Whom does the speaker blame for the change? Does that make him more sympathetic?
facilitatorNotes: Time, “the tyrant.” Blaming Time spares Amabel personal blame, yet he is still leaving her. Readers can debate whether the blame is generous or an excuse.
evidence: That Time the tyrant fell Ruled Amabel!

questions.prompt: He plans to “fling across the gate” a farewell lasting “Till the Last Trump.” Is this ending dignified, melodramatic or unkind?
facilitatorNotes: It is a grand farewell to someone still alive, and he has already reflected that “Love’s race” never runs short of new loves. Readers may find the gesture moving, theatrical or callous; Hardy may be letting us judge his young speaker.
evidence: But leave her to her fate
Knowing that, though Love cease, Love’s race shows undecrease

readings.title: Her Dilemma
readings.challenge: Follow a story compressed into four stanzas, and see why the last stanza turns from the woman’s choice to the world that forced it.
readings.focus: A kind lie at a deathbed, and a judgment on a world that makes such lies necessary.
readings.context: Thomas Hardy (1840–1928), best known for his novels of rural Wessex, his name for southwest England, published his first book of poems, Wessex Poems, in 1898; it gathers verse written over thirty years, some of it in the 1860s. This poem is dated 1866. A poppy-head is the carved top of a pew end in a church; “passed antique research” means too old even for scholars to date; “throughly” is thoroughly; “conditioned thus” means made this way.
readings.contentNote: A dying man asks a woman to say she loves him.

excerpt.locator: Her Dilemma (In — Church), the whole poem with its date; opens “THE two were silent in a sunless church, Whose mildewed walls, uneven paving-stones, And…”; closes “1866.”.

questions.prompt: How does the first stanza’s setting prepare for what happens? Find details of decay.
facilitatorNotes: The church is sunless, mildewed and worn, with uneven stones and carvings older than anyone can date, and the clock’s dull ticking counts time running out. The place, like the man, is wearing away.
evidence: Whose mildewed walls, uneven paving-stones
And nothing broke the clock’s dull monotones.

questions.prompt: Why does she lie? What does “worth her soul” suggest about how serious the lie is to her?
facilitatorNotes: She wishes she could say “yes” truly, and decides that a moment’s kindness to a dying man is worth even her soul. The lie costs her something she values deeply. Readers can debate whether it was right.
evidence: She would have given a world to breathe “yes” truly
’Twas worth her soul to be a moment kind.

questions.prompt: In the last stanza, whom or what does she blame, and why is she ashamed?
facilitatorNotes: Not the man or herself, but a world, or “Nature,” that devises such choices, where kindness requires a lie. She is ashamed to value life in a world made like that.
evidence: So mocked humanity that she shamed to prize A world conditioned thus
Where Nature such dilemmas could devise.

questions.prompt: The title calls it her dilemma. What exactly are her two choices, and does either come without a cost?
facilitatorNotes: Telling the truth would wound a dying man; comforting him requires a lie. Neither is free of cost, which is the point of the poem.
evidence: “Tell me you love me!”—holding hard her hand.

readings.title: She, to Him I and II
readings.challenge: Follow two long sentences, each building to a request or a realization at the end of a sonnet.
readings.focus: A woman foresees how her lover will remember her, and how unequal their memories will be.
readings.context: Thomas Hardy (1840–1928), best known for his novels of rural Wessex, his name for southwest England, published his first book of poems, Wessex Poems, in 1898; it gathers verse written over thirty years, some of it in the 1860s. These are the first two of four sonnets with this title, dated 1866, all spoken by a woman to the man she loves. In the first she imagines growing old; in the second, being dead. “The toils of Time” are Time’s nets; “lauded” means praised; a jade, said with pity, is a worn-out woman; a tittle is the smallest part; a masquerade is a masked ball.

excerpt.locator: She, to Him, sonnets I and II, each with its date; opens “WHEN you shall see me in the toils of Time, My lauded beauties carried off from me, My…”; closes “1866.”.

questions.prompt: Sonnet I is one long sentence beginning “When you shall see me.” What does she ask for at its end, and why does she insist that “with me lies not the blame”?
facilitatorNotes: She asks for his friendship when her beauty has gone. Time, a “Sportsman” who breeds his game only to kill it, is to blame, not her; she expects him to feel irritated and asks him to remember her unchanged soul.
evidence: Will you not grant to old affection’s claim The hand of friendship down Life’s sunless hill?
That Sportsman Time but rears his brood to kill

questions.prompt: “When in your being heart concedes to mind.” What does she fear will happen to his love?
facilitatorNotes: As feeling gives way to judgment, he will measure her against the “excellencies” she once had and be annoyed that they have withered. Love becomes an assessment.
evidence: When in your being heart concedes to mind
And you are irked that they have withered so

questions.prompt: In Sonnet II, what are the “two small words” he may think of her, and why does she call that thought “thin”?
facilitatorNotes: “Poor jade!”: a passing sigh of pity. For her, he was the whole of life; for him, she will be a brief thought. The inequality is the sonnet’s grief.
evidence: That your thin thought, in two small words conveyed
But the Whole Life wherein my part was played

questions.prompt: The final lines are hard: “And you amid its fitful masquerade / A Thought—as I in yours but seem to be.” How might you read them?
facilitatorNotes: One reading: he will never see that, in her life, he was the one great Thought amid its masked confusion, while she is only a slight thought in his. The capital letters of “Whole Life” and “Thought” support that contrast. Others hear “but seem” as a hope that she matters more to him than it appears. Accept readings that explain “seem.”
evidence: And you amid its fitful masquerade A Thought—as I in yours but seem to be.

readings.title: The Burghers
readings.challenge: Follow a story told in linked three-line stanzas, and decide what changes the speaker’s mind at the moment he could strike.
readings.focus: Revenge turned into a different, perhaps harsher, kind of justice.
readings.context: Thomas Hardy (1840–1928), best known for his novels of rural Wessex, his name for southwest England, published his first book of poems, Wessex Poems, in 1898; it gathers verse written over thirty years, some of it in the 1860s. The poem is set in the 1700s in Casterbridge, Hardy’s name for Dorchester. The speaker, a burgher (a prosperous townsman), learns that his wife plans to run away with her lover. Grey’s, Dammer’s Crest, the Froom and Glyd’path Rise are local places; “the Furnace” recalls the three men in the Book of Daniel who walked unharmed (“unshent”) in a fiery furnace; a pleasaunce is a garden; garde-robes are wardrobes; to cicatrize is to heal into a scar. The stanzas are terza rima: each middle line sets the rhyme of the next stanza.
readings.contentNote: A husband plans to kill his wife and her lover with a sword; the poem deals with adultery.

excerpt.locator: The Burghers (17–), the whole poem; opens “THE sun had wheeled from Grey’s to Dammer’s Crest, And still I mused on that Thing…”; closes “…carry wounds that none can cicatrize.” —“Not mortal?” said he. “Lingering—worse,” said I.”.

questions.prompt: The friend says, “Law consecrates the scheme.” What does he urge, and why does the speaker insist on going “alone”?
facilitatorNotes: The friend urges him to kill the pair as they flee, claiming the law would excuse a wronged husband. The speaker wants to act alone: out of pride, privacy, or perhaps because he is already unsure.
evidence: Law consecrates the scheme.
I’ll do it! But alone. I can be strong.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker see, when the lovers face him, that he had never seen before? How does it change him?
facilitatorNotes: Her look of complete love, given to the other man and never to him, and each lover trying to shield the other. He is “blanked” and sees himself as a “licensed tyrant” over two people bound by love.
evidence: Never upon me Had she thrown look of love so thorough-sped!
But licensed tyrant to this bonded pair?

questions.prompt: Why does he hand over the gold, jewels and robes she had left behind? Is this generosity, or something else?
facilitatorNotes: She had refused to take anything, so as not to rob him. His gift follows the rule of Charity he has just quoted. Some readers also see in it a way to bind the lovers by debt or to make himself the bigger person.
evidence: ’Twere base in me to rob my lord unware
I handed her the gold, her jewels all

questions.prompt: “I have struck well. They fly, / But carry wounds that none can cicatrize.” What wounds does he mean, and why are they “worse” than mortal?
facilitatorNotes: Wounds of conscience and obligation: they will live with his mercy, and that may hurt longer than a sword. Readers may hear a last bitterness that colours his generosity, or a way of saving face before his friend.
evidence: But carry wounds that none can cicatrize.
Lingering—worse

readings.title: The Peasant’s Confession
readings.challenge: Piece together a historical mystery from a confession, and weigh the speaker’s motives against the consequences.
readings.focus: A private choice, made to save a farm, that may have decided a battle.
readings.context: Thomas Hardy (1840–1928), best known for his novels of rural Wessex, his name for southwest England, published his first book of poems, Wessex Poems, in 1898; it gathers verse written over thirty years, some of it in the 1860s. On 18 June 1815 Napoleon was defeated at Waterloo, in present-day Belgium, by the British under Wellington and the Prussians under Blücher. His marshal Grouchy, with thirty thousand men, was following the Prussians and never arrived. The French epigraph, from the historian Thiers, says in substance: had the officer Napoleon sent to Grouchy the night before reached him, there would be no question; but he never arrived, as Grouchy always maintained, and no one has ever known whether he was captured or went over to the enemy. The speaker, a Belgian peasant, is confessing to a priest. The other names are places, commanders and officers of the battle; Landwehr were Prussian militia; “earing corn” is grain coming into ear.
readings.contentNote: The peasant kills a French officer with a sword, and the poem lists the dead of Waterloo.

excerpt.locator: The Peasant’s Confession, the whole poem with its French epigraph; opens ““Si le maréchal Grouchy avait été rejoint par l’officier que Napoléon lui avait expédié…”; closes “…And Virgin-Saint Marie; O Michael, John, and Holy Ones in rest, Entreat the Lord for me!”.

questions.prompt: How does the epigraph set up the poem?
facilitatorNotes: The historian ends on an open question: what became of the officer? The poem invents an answer, a confession that only the priest hears. Fiction fills a gap that history left.
evidence: C’est ce qu’on a toujours ignoré.

questions.prompt: How does the peasant reason before he misleads the officer? Which of his reasons are about his own farm?
facilitatorNotes: If Grouchy comes, the battle will be fought on his land and his farm stripped; the French have no money, while the English pay for what they take. Self-interest decides him.
evidence: My farm is stript. While, as for pieces three, Money the French have none.
They buy, not borrow.

questions.prompt: While the officer lies dead in the rye, the poem moves to the battlefield. How does Hardy link the private act to the battle?
facilitatorNotes: Napoleon waits for Grouchy, who never comes, and Grouchy is “mis-sent, blamed, yet blame-exempt.” We know what no one at Waterloo knew: why the order never arrived.
evidence: And yet he does not come!
mis-sent, blamed, yet blame-exempt

questions.prompt: Why does the poem list so many names of the dead, on both sides? What effect does the long list have?
facilitatorNotes: The jumble of French, British and German names makes the cost concrete and shared, and it weighs heavily against the peasant’s safe cow and hens.
evidence: And hosts of ranksmen round . . .
Safe was my stock; my capple cow unslain

questions.prompt: What exactly does the peasant regret, and is his confession wholly sincere? Look at the last three stanzas.
facilitatorNotes: He regrets betraying a cause he once favoured, and his old age is bitter: his children eye his store, a kind of punishment that mirrors his own greed. Some readers find real remorse; others hear self-pity mixed with it.
evidence: O Saints, had I but lost my earing corn And saved the cause once prized!
So now, being old, my children eye askance My slowly dwindling store

readings.title: The Dance at the Phœnix
readings.challenge: Follow a ballad’s story stanza by stanza, and listen for what the narrator leaves unsaid at the end.
readings.focus: One night’s return to youth, and its cost.
readings.context: Thomas Hardy (1840–1928), best known for his novels of rural Wessex, his name for southwest England, published his first book of poems, Wessex Poems, in 1898; it gathers verse written over thirty years, some of it in the 1860s. The poem is set in Casterbridge, Hardy’s name for Dorchester, after the wars with Napoleon. As a girl, Jenny had many sweethearts among the soldiers of the King’s-Own Cavalry stationed in the town; then she married a gentle, trusting countryman. The Phœnix was an inn; leazes are pastures; Parrett, Yeo and Tone are Somerset rivers; “blooth” is blossom; a cot is a cottage; Sirius is a bright star and the Wain the Plough (Big Dipper); “Soldier’s Joy” and the other titles are dance tunes; to “ray” is to dress; a durn is a doorpost.
readings.contentNote: The poem refers to a woman’s youthful love affairs and ends with her sudden death.

excerpt.locator: The Dance at the Phœnix, the whole poem; opens “TO Jenny came a gentle youth From inland leazes lone, His love was fresh as apple-blooth…”; closes “…they went from Casterbridge And vanished over Mellstock Ridge, ’Twas saddest morn to see.”.

questions.prompt: How does the poem describe Jenny’s marriage before the soldiers return? Which words show she has kept her vow?
facilitatorNotes: She kept herself “pure and just,” and even malice could find no sin in her. The narrator stresses her faithfulness, which makes the night’s temptation matter.
evidence: And Jenny kept her pure and just
No sin or sign of ill to be

questions.prompt: What draws Jenny out of bed? Find the lines where the music seems to work on her body.
facilitatorNotes: The tunes reach her in bed, and young blood seems to flood through her and sweep the years away; she walks to the inn with “tune-led feet.” The music acts almost like a spell.
evidence: Seemed scouring through her like a flood That whisked the years away.
She trod the flags with tune-led feet

questions.prompt: The sergeant calls her “Gay Granny”; the steward lets her in because they lack partners. What do these reactions show about how the soldiers see her?
facilitatorNotes: To them she is a comic old woman and a useful partner; they are a later generation and do not know her, though she “knew the regiment all.” Her memory and their indifference meet in one exchange.
evidence: “Gay Granny, whence come you?” he cried
I knew the regiment all!

questions.prompt: Her husband never learns where she went. What does the line “The King’s said not a word” add? Was their silence kind?
facilitatorNotes: The soldiers keep her secret, and her husband keeps his trust. Readers may find the silence kind, or think the husband’s trust is the poem’s saddest irony.
evidence: His Jenny had not left his side
The King’s said not a word.

questions.prompt: How would you describe the narrator’s attitude in the final stanza: disapproving, nostalgic, amused?
facilitatorNotes: “Times are not as times were then, / Nor fair ones half so free” could be a moral comment or a regret; calling the soldiers’ departure the “saddest morn” suggests the narrator shares Jenny’s nostalgia. Several readings hold.
evidence: Well! times are not as times were then, Nor fair ones half so free
’Twas saddest morn to see.

readings.title: Her Immortality
readings.challenge: Follow a conversation with a ghost and work out the strange logic by which she survives.
readings.focus: The dead live only in the memory of the living.
readings.context: Thomas Hardy (1840–1928), best known for his novels of rural Wessex, his name for southwest England, published his first book of poems, Wessex Poems, in 1898; it gathers verse written over thirty years, some of it in the 1860s. The speaker visits the place where he last saw a woman he loved, who has died; her husband has since remarried. A shade is a ghost; a “sprite” is a spirit; “ball or blade” means a bullet or a knife; to “surcease” is to come to an end; the “seasons’ ingresses” are the first days of the seasons.
readings.contentNote: The grieving speaker says he will kill himself to join the dead woman; her ghost persuades him to live.

excerpt.locator: Her Immortality, the whole poem; opens “UPON a noon I pilgrimed through A pasture, mile by mile, Unto the place where I last saw…”; closes “…Through whom alone lives she, Ceases my Love, her words, her ways, Never again to be!”.

questions.prompt: What has happened to the woman’s memory among her family and friends? Why does this matter to what she says next?
facilitatorNotes: Her husband has remarried, her children love the new wife, and her family and friends avoid her spirit. Only the speaker remembers her, which is why his life matters to her.
evidence: My husband clasps another bride
Who prized me most I did not know Till I passed down from sight.

questions.prompt: How does the ghost answer his plan to join her? Explain “By living, me you keep alive, / By dying you slay me.”
facilitatorNotes: A shade lives only in those who remember it; if he dies, she ends with him. Death would not reunite them: it would finish her.
evidence: A Shade but in its mindful ones Has immortality
By living, me you keep alive, By dying you slay me.

questions.prompt: How does the speaker change after her words? Is the change hopeful?
facilitatorNotes: He gives up his wish to die and will guard himself from every harm, but he still calls life a “bleak unrest.” He now has a reason to live, which is not the same as happiness.
evidence: Dismissing late distaste for life, I craved its bleak unrest.
I’ll guard me from minutest harms

questions.prompt: The last stanza begins “But grows my grief.” Why might his grief grow even though she keeps visiting him?
facilitatorNotes: He knows that she will end when he does, so each visit reminds him how fragile she is. Remembering keeps her, and it is also a burden. Readers may connect this with their own ways of remembering people.
evidence: But grows my grief.
Ceases my Love, her words, her ways, Never again to be!

readings.title: Friends Beyond
readings.challenge: Hear several voices from a churchyard, and decide what the dead have gained and lost.
readings.focus: The peace of the dead as freedom from caring.
readings.context: Thomas Hardy (1840–1928), best known for his novels of rural Wessex, his name for southwest England, published his first book of poems, Wessex Poems, in 1898; it gathers verse written over thirty years, some of it in the 1860s. Mellstock is Hardy’s name for Stinsford, the Dorset parish where he grew up; William Dewy and Tranter Reuben appear in his novel Under the Greenwood Tree. Some of the dead speak Dorset dialect: “mid” means might, “wold” old, “vallie” value, “zell” sell, and “ho” fret; charlock is a weed; grinterns are the bins of a granary. A tranter is a carrier; leads are lead roofs; stillicide is dripping water; to “quire” is to sing in the church choir; the Trine is the Holy Trinity.

excerpt.locator: Friends Beyond, the whole poem; opens “WILLIAM DEWY, Tranter Reuben, Farmer Ledlow late at plough, Robert’s kin, and John’s, and…”; closes “…kin, and John’s, and Ned’s, And the Squire, and Lady Susan, murmur mildly to me now.”.

questions.prompt: What do the dead say they have “triumphed” over? Is it a happy triumph?
facilitatorNotes: Death has freed them from need, criticism and even the fear of death: “a morrow free of thought.” It is also the loss of all caring, so the triumph can sound peaceful or chilling.
evidence: We have triumphed: this achievement turns the bane to antidote
Fear of death has even bygone us: death gave all that we possess.

questions.prompt: Each of the dead allows the living to do something that would once have hurt. Choose two. What do they reveal about the speakers’ lives?
facilitatorNotes: William Dewy’s beloved bass-viol, the Squire’s wife and good name, Lady Susan’s letters, the farmer’s heifer, the wife’s best china: small treasures and deep attachments, now released without a pang.
evidence: Ye mid burn the wold bass-viol that I set such vallie by.
If ye break my best blue china, children, I shan’t care or ho.

questions.prompt: The dead are not curious whether “you quire to our old tune.” How might the living speaker feel on hearing that?
facilitatorNotes: The living keep up old ways partly to honour the dead, and the dead do not care. That could hurt, or it could free the living to change. The poem leaves the speaker’s feelings unstated.
evidence: Curious not the least are we if our intents you make or mar
If you quire to our old tune

questions.prompt: The poem begins and ends with almost the same lines. What has changed between “lie in Mellstock churchyard now” and “murmur mildly to me now”?
facilitatorNotes: The dead go from lying silent to speaking. The frame encloses their voices, and in between they have gained “very gods’ composure”: the calm of beings no longer touched by anything.
evidence: lie in Mellstock churchyard now!
murmur mildly to me now.

readings.title: Thoughts of Phena
readings.challenge: Follow questions the speaker cannot answer, and notice how the ending turns the opening complaint around.
readings.focus: Remembering someone only as she was, for lack of any later trace.
readings.context: Thomas Hardy (1840–1928), best known for his novels of rural Wessex, his name for southwest England, published his first book of poems, Wessex Poems, in 1898; it gathers verse written over thirty years, some of it in the 1860s. This poem is dated March 1890. Biographers usually identify Phena as Hardy’s cousin Tryphena Sparks, whom he knew well when both were young and who died that year. A dame is a married woman; an “aureate nimb” is a golden halo; “fined” means refined or purified.

excerpt.locator: Thoughts of Phena, at News of Her Death, the whole poem with its date; opens “NOT a line of her writing have I, Not a thread of her hair, No mark of her late time as…”; closes “_March_ 1890.”.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker lack, and why does it trouble him?
facilitatorNotes: No letter, no lock of hair, no sign of her life as a married woman: nothing to help him picture her last years. He tries, “in vain,” to imagine her at the end.
evidence: a line of her writing have I, Not a thread of her hair
And in vain do I urge my unsight

questions.prompt: The second stanza asks about her last days. What are the two possibilities, and why can he not choose between them?
facilitatorNotes: Either her kindness surrounded her like a golden halo, or misfortune, regret and fear dimmed her. He simply does not know her later life.
evidence: With an aureate nimb?
unease, or regret, or forebodings, or fears Disennoble her soul?

questions.prompt: The last stanza repeats the opening lines. How has their meaning changed?
facilitatorNotes: At first the lack of relics is a loss. By the end it may be why he keeps “the best of her”: the young woman, purified in memory. Readers may see consolation, or a choice not to know.
evidence: yet haply the best of her—fined in my brain It maybe the more
Thus I do but the phantom retain

questions.prompt: Long lines alternate with short, indented ones. How does that shape suit the poem?
facilitatorNotes: The long lines search; the short ones stop, almost like a breath catching. The pattern returns like the memory itself.
evidence: Sad, shining, or dim?

readings.title: Nature’s Questioning
readings.challenge: Sort the possible explanations the poem offers, and notice that the speaker accepts none of them.
readings.focus: Nature as puzzled schoolchildren, asking why they exist.
readings.context: Thomas Hardy (1840–1928), best known for his novels of rural Wessex, his name for southwest England, published his first book of poems, Wessex Poems, in 1898; it gathers verse written over thirty years, some of it in the 1860s. Hardy, who lost his religious faith as a young man, often asked in his poems what kind of power, if any, governs the world. “Lippings” are faint movements of the lips; “hazardry” is chance; an Automaton is a machine that acts without thought; Godhead means God; a Forlorn Hope is a band of soldiers sent first into an attack, expecting to die.
readings.contentNote: The poem questions the existence and nature of God.

excerpt.locator: Nature’s Questioning, the whole poem; opens “WHEN I look forth at dawning, pool, Field, flock, and lonely tree, All seem to gaze at me…”; closes “…Earth’s old glooms and pains Are still the same, and gladdest Life Death neighbours nigh.”.

questions.prompt: The pool, field, flock and tree look at the speaker “Like chastened children sitting silent in a school.” What does the simile suggest about their “master”?
facilitatorNotes: A harsh teacher has dulled them over long days and crushed their first delight in being alive. Nature itself seems worn down.
evidence: Like chastened children sitting silent in a school
Their first terrestrial zest had chilled and overborne.

questions.prompt: List the explanations nature wonders about. Which is the most hopeful, and how hopeful is it?
facilitatorNotes: A “Vast Imbecility” that made and abandoned them; an unconscious machine; the remains of a dying God; or a high Plan of Good overcoming Evil. Even the last makes them the Forlorn Hope, sacrificed for a victory others will see.
evidence: Has some Vast Imbecility
Or come we of an Automaton
We the Forlorn Hope over which Achievement strides?

questions.prompt: “No answerer I.” Why does the speaker not answer, and what does the poem give instead?
facilitatorNotes: He does not know. Instead he records what goes on: wind, rain, old glooms and pains, and death always next to life. The facts do not settle the question.
evidence: Thus things around. No answerer I . . .
and gladdest Life Death neighbours nigh.

questions.prompt: Is the poem despairing? Find evidence on both sides.
facilitatorNotes: Its possibilities are bleak and its ending gloomy, but nature’s “wonder” and the speaker’s refusal to give false answers can seem honest rather than hopeless. Readers may weigh these differently.
evidence: We wonder, ever wonder, why we find us here!
Are still the same

readings.title: The Impercipient
readings.challenge: Follow an argument made through comparisons, and notice what the speaker asks of the believers around him.
readings.focus: Unbelief felt as a loss, not a victory.
readings.context: Thomas Hardy (1840–1928), best known for his novels of rural Wessex, his name for southwest England, published his first book of poems, Wessex Poems, in 1898; it gathers verse written over thirty years, some of it in the 1860s. “Impercipient” means one who does not perceive. The speaker sits in a cathedral among worshippers whose faith he cannot share. “Infelicity” is unhappiness; “liefer” means rather; “meet” means fitting. The row of asterisks is printed in the poem.
readings.contentNote: The poem is about lacking religious faith; it describes the speaker’s isolation without mocking believers.

excerpt.locator: The Impercipient (At a Cathedral Service), the whole poem; opens “THAT from this bright believing band An outcast I should be, That faiths by which my…”; closes “Enough. As yet disquiet clings About us. Rest shall we.”.

questions.prompt: How does the speaker feel about not sharing the faith around him? Which words show he does not feel superior?
facilitatorNotes: He calls it a “drear destiny” and “infelicity,” sees himself as an outcast and speaks of “my lack.” Unbelief feels like a deprivation, not a victory.
evidence: Is a drear destiny.
My lack might move their sympathies

questions.prompt: Explain the comparison in the fourth stanza. Who hears the sea, and what does the speaker hear?
facilitatorNotes: An inland group hears “the glorious distant sea”; he hears only wind in a dark pine. The same sound means different things to different listeners, and the poem does not say who is right.
evidence: The glorious distant sea!
’tis but yon dark And wind-swept pine to me!

questions.prompt: What charge does he object to in the fifth stanza, and how does the bird answer it?
facilitatorNotes: Believers accuse him of preferring that blessed things did not exist. A bird without wings does not stay on the ground by choice: he cannot help his blindness.
evidence: But for the charge that blessed things I’d liefer have unbe.
O, doth a bird deprived of wings Go earth-bound wilfully!

questions.prompt: After the asterisks the poem ends: “Enough. As yet disquiet clings / About us. Rest shall we.” Who is “us,” and why break off?
facilitatorNotes: “Us” may be the speaker and the believers together: all share unrest, and all will rest, perhaps in death. The break suggests that argument is useless, and the ending sounds like a truce.
evidence: As yet disquiet clings About us. Rest shall we.

readings.title: In a Eweleaze near Weatherbury
readings.challenge: Compare what Time has changed with what the speaker insists has not.
readings.focus: An aging body and a heart that stays young.
readings.context: Thomas Hardy (1840–1928), best known for his novels of rural Wessex, his name for southwest England, published his first book of poems, Wessex Poems, in 1898; it gathers verse written over thirty years, some of it in the 1860s. A eweleaze (or leaze) is a sheep pasture; Weatherbury is Hardy’s name for the Dorset village of Puddletown. The poem is dated 1890, when Hardy was fifty. “Ghast and grizzel” means ghastly pale and grey; a blazon is a coat of arms, here his youthful looks; to “balm the breeze” is to sweeten the air.

excerpt.locator: In a Eweleaze near Weatherbury, the whole poem with its date; opens “THE years have gathered grayly Since I danced upon this leaze With one who kindled gaily…”; closes “1890.”.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker say has not changed in him, despite “the term as teacher”?
facilitatorNotes: His fantasies and his love of beauty are what they were when he danced here. Years of experience did not teach him to want differently.
evidence: I remain what I was then In each essential feature Of the fantasies of men.

questions.prompt: How does Hardy picture Time in the second stanza? Why is the image unsettling?
facilitatorNotes: Time is a craftsman with a little chisel who never sleeps, defacing the speaker’s looks and secretly boring into his bones at night, storing up pains. It is patient, physical and sly.
evidence: Yet I note the little chisel Of never-napping Time
I feel him boring sly Within my bones

questions.prompt: Who is “Beauty” in the last stanza, and why would she “scorn my brave endeavour”?
facilitatorNotes: Both the girl he danced with and beauty itself. He would still give up duty for her, but she would not answer an aging man as she did then. The change is in her reply, not his desire.
evidence: Still, I’d go the world with Beauty
But she’d scorn my brave endeavour

questions.prompt: He would “shun divinest duty” for Beauty. Is his refusal to grow old in spirit admirable, foolish or both?
facilitatorNotes: Readers may see vitality or vanity. The quick, dancing rhythm suggests that Hardy smiles at himself even as he feels the loss.
evidence: I would shun divinest duty To resume her worshipping.

readings.title: Heiress and Architect
readings.challenge: Follow a dialogue in which every request meets a refusal, and find the pattern in the architect’s last lines.
readings.focus: Youthful hopes meet a designer who builds for decline and death.
readings.context: Thomas Hardy (1840–1928), best known for his novels of rural Wessex, his name for southwest England, published his first book of poems, Wessex Poems, in 1898; it gathers verse written over thirty years, some of it in the 1860s. Hardy trained and worked as an architect before he became a writer; the poem, dated 1867, is dedicated to A. W. B., the London architect Arthur Blomfield, for whom he worked in the 1860s. Tracery is ornamental stonework in windows; ogive-work is pointed Gothic arches; a zephyr is a soft breeze; “engrailed” means edged with a scalloped pattern; to “hale” is to haul.
readings.contentNote: The poem ends with a coffin carried down the stairs.

excerpt.locator: Heiress and Architect, for A. W. B., the whole poem with its date; opens “SHE sought the Studios, beckoning to her side An arch-designer, for she planned to build.…”; closes “1867.”.

questions.prompt: List the four things the heiress asks for. How do her requests change from first to last?
facilitatorNotes: High open halls full of scent and birdsong; wide glass fronts to show her light; a little chamber for meeting her love; finally a narrow turret where she can grieve alone. Her hopes shrink from joy to private sorrow.
evidence: high halls with tracery
wide fronts of crystal glass
A little chamber, then, with swan and dove
Some narrow winding turret, quite mine own

questions.prompt: Each of the architect’s answers ends with a short line beginning “For.” What are the four, and what do they add up to?
facilitatorNotes: Winters freeze; you will tire; you will fade; you will die. The refrain marches from weather to death, the end every building must allow for.
evidence: For winters freeze.
For you will tire.
For you will fade.
For you will die.

questions.prompt: How does Hardy describe the architect’s manner? Is he wise, cruel or both?
facilitatorNotes: He has a “cold, clear voice, and cold, clear view,” nothing warms him, and he has a “measuring eye.” Everything he says is true, and he crushes every hope. Readers can argue for wisdom, cruelty, or both at once.
evidence: With cold, clear voice, and cold, clear view
Said he, the man of measuring eye

questions.prompt: Why might the architect stand for something larger than an architect? What might the house represent?
facilitatorNotes: The house can be her life, and the architect Time, Reason or Necessity, the power that plans for “vicissitudes” and “swayed her like a shade.” The poem reads as an allegory as well as a scene.
evidence: The man who swayed her like a shade.
For such vicissitudes as living brings

readings.title: “I Look into My Glass”
readings.challenge: Read a very short poem slowly, and find the single wish the whole poem turns on.
readings.focus: A body that ages and a heart that does not.
readings.context: Thomas Hardy (1840–1928), best known for his novels of rural Wessex, his name for southwest England, published his first book of poems, Wessex Poems, in 1898; it gathers verse written over thirty years, some of it in the 1860s. This is the last poem in the book. A glass is a mirror. “Equanimity” is calm evenness of mind; “noontide” is midday.

excerpt.locator: “I Look into My Glass,” the whole poem, the last in Wessex Poems; opens “I LOOK into my glass, And view my wasting skin, And say, “Would God it came to pass My…”; closes “…lets part abide; And shakes this fragile frame at eve With throbbings of noontide.”.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker wish when he sees his “wasting skin”? Why would that make old age easier?
facilitatorNotes: That his heart had shrunk as thin as his skin. With less feeling, the coldness of others would not hurt him, and he could wait for death calmly.
evidence: My heart had shrunk as thin!
Could lonely wait my endless rest With equanimity.

questions.prompt: What does Time do instead? Explain “Part steals, lets part abide.”
facilitatorNotes: It takes the body’s youth and leaves the feelings, and the poem says it does so “to make me grieve.” The mismatch is the pain.
evidence: Part steals, lets part abide

questions.prompt: “This fragile frame at eve” is shaken “With throbbings of noontide.” What do evening and noon stand for, and why is the clash painful?
facilitatorNotes: Evening is old age, noon the prime of life. Strong feelings shake a body too frail for them; the image is almost physical.
evidence: And shakes this fragile frame at eve With throbbings of noontide.

questions.prompt: The poem uses three short stanzas and plain rhymes. Does the simple form make the feeling stronger or weaker?
facilitatorNotes: Many readers find the restraint powerful: a strong feeling held in a plain, hymn-like shape. Others may find it understated. Ask readers to point to a line where the plainness works.
evidence: And view my wasting skin

readings.title: The Alarm
readings.challenge: Follow a soldier’s argument with himself, and decide what you think of the sign that settles it.
readings.focus: Love, duty and the wish for a sign from heaven, in a false alarm of war.
readings.context: Thomas Hardy (1840–1928), best known for his novels of rural Wessex, his name for southwest England, published his first book of poems, Wessex Poems, in 1898; it gathers verse written over thirty years, some of it in the 1860s. In 1803 Britain expected Napoleon (spelled Buonaparte here) to invade from France; volunteers trained to defend the coast, and beacons on the hills were to be lit if the French landed. Hardy’s novel The Trumpet-Major is set in those years. “Royal George’s town” is Weymouth, the seaside town that King George III often visited; Horatio Nelson was Britain’s great admiral. A croft is a small farm; “broached the spiced and brewed” means opened the drink; to antedate is to come early; a char-wench is a serving girl; the Road is an anchorage off the coast; a firelock is a musket; to palter is to waver or bargain; “childing” means expecting a child; remission is forgiveness; Holy Writ is the Bible; “wist” means knew; Te Deum is a hymn of thanksgiving.

excerpt.locator: The Alarm (1803), the whole poem with its note and dedication; opens “_See_ “_The Trumpet-Major_””; closes “…with wife and friends: “We praise Thee, Lord, discerning That Thou hast helped in this!””.

questions.prompt: What does the Volunteer’s farewell speech show about him? Look at how it ends.
facilitatorNotes: He is practical and caring, arranging food and help for the birth, and he makes light of the danger (“He’s not like to land!”) to calm his wife. The long list of kit ends with the one thing he cannot take: his heart. The joke hides how much the parting costs him.
evidence: He’s not like to land!
My heart, Dear; that must stay!

questions.prompt: When he sees the beacon and hears that Napoleon has anchored, what does he consider doing, and how does he argue for it?
facilitatorNotes: He thinks of going back to hide his wife in the woods. He argues that she will think he lied about the danger, and that the sin of deserting to save “a childing wife” would be forgiven by Christ, though not by men. The poem treats his temptation with sympathy.
evidence: Seek the woods with her till times have altered;
Such sin, to save a childing wife, would earn it Christ’s remission,

questions.prompt: How does the bird decide him? Does the poem present it as a real sign from God, or as what the soldier believes?
facilitatorNotes: He frees a bird tangled in the river weed and asks God to guide its flight; it flies south toward the coast, and he marches on. Hardy keeps a little distance: the bird flies “as if surmising,” it “seemed him” Heaven sent it, and he was prompted, “he wist,” by God. Readers can argue for either view.
evidence: till it seemed him Heaven had pleased it As guide to send the bird.
Prompted he wist by Whom.

questions.prompt: Napoleon never comes. How do you read the ending: as sincere thanksgiving, as irony, or both?
facilitatorNotes: The Volunteer marched to a battle that never happened and thanks God for the outcome. A reader can see a quiet, sincere family memory (the poem is dedicated to one of Hardy’s family), or irony in a sign that “worked” whatever happened. The modest happy ending lets both stand.
evidence: But Buonaparte still tarried;
That Thou hast helped in this!

readings.title: A Sign-Seeker
readings.challenge: Divide the poem into what the speaker can see and know and what he longs for and cannot find.
readings.focus: A searcher who knows the natural world well and finds no sign beyond it.
readings.context: Thomas Hardy (1840–1928), best known for his novels of rural Wessex, his name for southwest England, published his first book of poems, Wessex Poems, in 1898; it gathers verse written over thirty years, some of it in the 1860s. Hardy wrote many poems questioning religious belief. “Liveries” are uniforms, here the seasons’ colors; “subtrude” means creep in; eccentric orbs are comets; to mete is to measure; “moils” are toils and struggles; “fain would wot of” means would gladly know; “vouchsafed” means granted; “unheed” means those who do not seek; “Writ” is the Bible; to “inscroll” is to write in a record; Nescience is not-knowing.
readings.contentNote: The speaker longs for signs of life after death and finds none. Discuss this as his view, alongside the believers he describes in the poem.

excerpt.locator: A Sign-Seeker, the whole poem; opens “I MARK the months in liveries dank and dry, The noontides many-shaped and hued; I see the…”; closes “…To open out my limitings, And Nescience mutely muses: When a man falls he lies.”.

questions.prompt: The first five stanzas list what the speaker has seen and learned. What kinds of knowledge are they?
facilitatorNotes: The weather and seasons, storms, earthquakes and volcanoes, the science of astronomy (predicting eclipses, weighing the sun), and human life with its meetings, sorrows and deaths: everything the senses and science can reach. He is no careless observer.
evidence: I learn to prophesy the hid eclipse,
—All the vast various moils that mean a world alive.

questions.prompt: What three signs does he long for in stanzas VII to IX?
facilitatorNotes: A dead parent or friend appearing by a grave to say “Not the end!”; some mark proving that the kisses of a dead love in dreams are real; and a heavenly “Recorder” dropping a feather to show that wrongs done to the weak are written down. Each would prove that death or injustice is not final.
evidence: Wearing his smile, and “Not the end!”
And drop one plume as pledge that Heaven inscrolls the wrong.

questions.prompt: How does the speaker describe people who believe they do see such signs? Is he mocking them, envying them, or both?
facilitatorNotes: They are “rapt to heights of trancéd trust” and read “radiant hints.” The words are not unkind and may be envious: “Such scope is granted not to lives like mine.” Some readers hear a hint of doubt about their trance; others hear simple longing.
evidence: There are who, rapt to heights of trancéd trust,
Such scope is granted not to lives like mine . . .

questions.prompt: “When a man falls he lies.” What does the last line mean, and why does Hardy give it to “Nescience”?
facilitatorNotes: A fallen man stays down: death is the end. But the speaker gives the words to Nescience, not-knowing, which “mutely muses,” so the line is less a proof than the silence of an unanswered question. Readers can debate whether the ending is despair or honesty.
evidence: And Nescience mutely muses: When a man falls he lies.

readings.title: At an Inn
readings.challenge: Work out what the people at the inn believed, what was true, and what has changed since.
readings.focus: A love that came too late, and the gap between seeming and being.
readings.context: Thomas Hardy (1840–1928), best known for his novels of rural Wessex, his name for southwest England, published his first book of poems, Wessex Poems, in 1898; it gathers verse written over thirty years, some of it in the 1860s. “Catering care” means service with food and drink; to opine is to suppose; “quicks” means brings to life; “the spheres above” are the heavens; to flush is to light up; a pane-fly is a fly buzzing at a window; “palsied” means numbed; “port” here means bearing or appearance; “after-hours” means later times.

excerpt.locator: At an Inn, the whole poem; opens “WHEN we as strangers sought Their catering care, Veiled smiles bespoke their thought Of…”; closes “…O severing sea and land, O laws of men, Ere death, once let us stand As we stood then!”.

questions.prompt: What did the people at the inn think about the pair, and how did that make them behave?
facilitatorNotes: They guessed the two were lovers who had given up everything for love, and they warmed to them, served them gladly and wished such happiness for themselves. Their kindness rested on a mistake.
evidence: They warmed as they opined Us more than friends—
“Ah, God, that bliss like theirs Would flush our day!”

questions.prompt: What actually happened when the two were left alone? Which images show it?
facilitatorNotes: Nothing: “never the love-light shone.” A chill falls on the afternoon and even numbs the buzzing fly. Love was present but “lingered-numb,” held back.
evidence: Yet never the love-light shone Between us there!
And palsied unto death The pane-fly’s tune.

questions.prompt: Explain the last stanza’s reversal: “As we seemed we were not … And now we seem not what / We aching are.”
facilitatorNotes: Then they looked like lovers and were not; now they are in love and cannot show it. The speaker blames Love for making sport of them, and “severing sea and land” and “laws of men” now keep them apart: perhaps distance, perhaps marriage. The poem leaves the obstacle unexplained.
evidence: As we seemed we were not That day afar,
O severing sea and land, O laws of men,

questions.prompt: The poem uses very short lines and a regular rhyme. How does the form suit a story of feelings held back?
facilitatorNotes: The clipped lines sound restrained, like people who cannot say what they feel; the final wish (“once let us stand / As we stood then!”) breaks out with more force after so much control. Some readers find the form too neat for such pain; the evidence supports either view.
evidence: Ere death, once let us stand As we stood then!

readings.title: The Fire at Tranter Sweatley’s
readings.challenge: Read the dialect aloud to catch the words, and decide how the poem wants you to feel at each turn.
readings.focus: A comic ballad built on a forced marriage and a fatal fire.
readings.context: Thomas Hardy (1840–1928), best known for his novels of rural Wessex, his name for southwest England, published his first book of poems, Wessex Poems, in 1898; it gathers verse written over thirty years, some of it in the 1860s. This ballad is written in Dorset dialect; reading it aloud helps. A tranter is a carrier who moves people’s goods; Zundays are Sundays; junketings are merry-makings; a “thirtover” uncle is a stubborn one; a goodman is a husband; a gaffer is an old man; “sommat” is something; reading the names “over pu’pit” is announcing a marriage in church; a linhay is an open shed; vlankers are sparks; a chimley-tun is a chimney top; an orchet is an orchard; lewth is shelter; a codlin-tree is an apple tree; bivering is shivering; a night-rail is a nightgown; totties are feet; gallied means frightened; “en” means him; a weir-hatch holds back water; “mid” means might; “thik husbird” is a coarse insult, roughly “that wretch”; nater is nature; a chiel is a child; mixens are dung heaps; shrammed means numb with cold; clouts are clothes; a tallet is a hayloft; a skimmington-ride was a noisy procession to shame people thought to have broken the rules of marriage; “wold” is old.
readings.contentNote: A young woman is forced to marry a drunken older man, who dies in a fire on the wedding night while she escapes in her nightgown. The poem treats this as rough comedy, and ends with a joke about her still being “a maiden.” “Gipsy” is a period word for the Roma people.

excerpt.locator: The Fire at Tranter Sweatley’s, the whole poem with its dates; opens “THEY had long met o’ Zundays—her true love and she— And at junketings, maypoles, and…”; closes “_Written_ 1866; _printed_ 1875.”.

questions.prompt: How does the first stanza set up the story? What do we learn about the uncle and about Tranter Sweatley?
facilitatorNotes: Barbree and her true love have courted for a long time, but her stubborn uncle insists she marry Sweatley, an old man “oft weak at the knee” from drink. The comic rhymes make the injustice sound like a joke, which is the poem’s method throughout.
evidence: But she bode wi’ a thirtover uncle,
From taking o’ sommat more cheerful than tea—

questions.prompt: Barbree’s speech piles up her troubles: “And then, upon top o’ that…” Is this moment funny, sad, or both?
facilitatorNotes: Both: her misery is real (“slave to thik husbird for bread”), but the repetition builds like a comic list and ends with being “burnt out o’ bed.” The poem invites laughter without mocking her; she is the one telling the joke.
evidence: And then, upon top o’ that, burnt out o’ bed,
Is more than my nater can stand!”

questions.prompt: When the neighbors search the ruins, “all they could find was a bone.” Why do the uncle and Barbree react as they do? How does the poem treat the husband’s death?
facilitatorNotes: The uncle is terrified and begins to repent, since his forcing of the marriage led to this; Barbree stays hidden “till sure she was free.” The death is handled lightly, almost as a convenient accident, which some readers find shocking and others accept as the rough justice of a folk ballad.
evidence: And all they could find was a bone.
But before ’twas complete, and till sure she was free,

questions.prompt: How does the community respond when it learns where Barbree is hiding? What does the ending suggest about who controls her life?
facilitatorNotes: First a skimmington-ride shames the pair; then “decent people” decide they should marry. Barbree finally speaks up for herself, insisting she stands “as a maiden”: her first marriage never counted. Her uncle and her neighbors have decided her marriages, yet the last word is hers.
evidence: Saying Tim and his lodger should risk it, and pair:
I stand as a maiden to-day!”

readings.title: The Two Men
readings.challenge: Lay the two lives side by side, stage by stage, and test the moralists’ last line.
readings.focus: Ideals, idleness and how the world judges by results.
readings.context: Thomas Hardy (1840–1928), best known for his novels of rural Wessex, his name for southwest England, published his first book of poems, Wessex Poems, in 1898; it gathers verse written over thirty years, some of it in the 1860s. Hardy dated this poem 1866, when he was a young architect in London writing poems in his spare time. The Market is the world of business and money-making; “mortal lot” is human life; “meaner mould” means lower purposes; a “plighted one” is a fiancée; “fain” means willing; a mart is a market; a “privy lair” is a hiding place; “descried” means caught sight of; “much corn and wine” is wealth; a pauper is someone too poor to live without charity; “dust to dust” comes from the burial service.

excerpt.locator: The Two Men, the whole poem with its date; opens “THERE were two youths of equal age, Wit, station, strength, and parentage; They studied…”; closes “1866.”.

questions.prompt: What does the first young man choose, and what does it cost him?
facilitatorNotes: He rejects the “sordid war” of business to work in secret for Truth and Purity, hoping people will support him. His garden runs wild, he loses hope, and he dies poor and friendless. His powers could have made him rich had he used them on “things of meaner mould.”
evidence: To rate the Market’s sordid war As something scarce worth living for.
And drooped to death in poverty . . .

questions.prompt: Why does the first man pretend to his love that he is tired of her? Is it noble or mistaken?
facilitatorNotes: He wants her to scorn him and leave quickly, so that she will not suffer in his ruin: angry love dies fast, but starved love lingers. It is self-sacrifice, but it also destroys the hope that kept him alive. Readers may admire it or think he decided for her.
evidence: I cannot kiss: I tire of thee!
For incensed love breathes quick and dies,

questions.prompt: How does the second man’s story mirror the first? Find the matching stages.
facilitatorNotes: Both shut themselves away and neglect their dress; both seek support from others; both visit their love by night and give her up; both die paupers without friends. But the second man is lazy and wants to marry money, and his love “read him.” The parallel stanzas make the contrast in motives sharp.
evidence: How he might live by doing nought.
But this Fair read him;

questions.prompt: “These men were like in all they did.” Are the moralists right? What is Hardy’s point?
facilitatorNotes: Judged by outcomes they look alike: two failures in pauper graves. But their reasons and their love were opposite. The irony is that the world, which judges by results, cannot see the difference; readers may also wonder whether Hardy thinks the idealist’s choice was worth it.
evidence: “These men were like in all they did.”

readings.title: Ditty (E. L. G.)
readings.challenge: Follow a refrain through five stanzas, and notice where the love song admits a doubt.
readings.focus: Love as something only the lover can see, and the part chance plays in it.
readings.context: Thomas Hardy (1840–1928), best known for his novels of rural Wessex, his name for southwest England, published his first book of poems, Wessex Poems, in 1898; it gathers verse written over thirty years, some of it in the 1860s. E. L. G. are the initials of Emma Lavinia Gifford, whom Hardy met in 1870, the date printed at the end, while he was working as an architect in a remote part of Cornwall; they married in 1874. A ditty is a simple song. A knap is a small hill; the firstling is the first-born lamb or calf of the season; to browse is to graze on leaves; a fabric here is a building; fellow-wights are fellow men; to descry is to make out; a legend here is an inscription; “by rote” means by heart; nought means nothing, of no importance; bond-servants are slaves; errant means wandering; to out-skirt a place is to pass round its edge.

excerpt.locator: Ditty (E. L. G.), the whole poem with its date; opens “BENEATH a knap where flown Nestlings play, Within walls of weathered stone, Far away From…”; closes “1870.”.

questions.prompt: Each stanza ends “Where she dwells.” What kind of place is it, according to the first stanza?
facilitatorNotes: Remote and old: under a small hill, weathered stone walls, nestlings and young animals, far from rows of formal houses, where “no man barters, no man sells.” It stands outside the world of trade and show.
evidence: From the files of formal houses,
No man barters, no man sells

questions.prompt: What does the speaker see written on the house that his neighbours cannot? What does this suggest about love?
facilitatorNotes: “Here is she!” seems written everywhere, for him alone; to others the building shows no such inscription. Love changes what a person sees: the place is special only through her.
evidence: Seems written everywhere
No such lucid legend tells

questions.prompt: Stanza IV admits something uncomfortable. What is the “smart severe,” and what makes it “severer”?
facilitatorNotes: The sting is the thought that, had he never wandered near her, he might have loved someone else as truly and never missed her. Worse, she is “nought,” no one important, outside her own valley, just as he is. Some readers find this unromantic; others find it more honest than most love songs.
evidence: To feel I might have kissed—
In the thought that she is nought,

questions.prompt: How does the last stanza answer stanza IV’s doubt? Is the final exclamation convincing?
facilitatorNotes: We are all “bond-servants of Chance”: he found her only because his wandering path did not skirt that spot. Yet he still calls it the spot “That no spot on earth excels.” Knowing his love came by chance, he chooses it anyway. Readers may hear triumph, or a bittersweet note under it.
evidence: What bond-servants of Chance
That no spot on earth excels,

readings.title: The Casterbridge Captains
readings.challenge: Watch a survivor’s view of his own success change in eight short stanzas.
readings.focus: Chance, survival and the glory given to the dead.
readings.context: Thomas Hardy (1840–1928), best known for his novels of rural Wessex, his name for southwest England, published his first book of poems, Wessex Poems, in 1898; it gathers verse written over thirty years, some of it in the 1860s. The heading names a place and year, the Khyber Pass, 1842: in the First Anglo-Afghan War a British army retreating from Kabul was almost wiped out, and other British forces fought through the Khyber Pass between Afghanistan and India. Casterbridge is Hardy’s name for Dorchester, his home town; the subtitle calls the poem a local “tradition” and names the three captains only by initials. “Of yore” means from long ago; laurels are a victor’s wreath; an aisle is part of a church; “untrumped of fame” means not yet famous; pupilage is being a schoolboy; “unweeting” means unaware; “stayed” here means stopped, killed; “sphered” means surrounded; transcendent means rising above the ordinary; an urn holds a dead person’s ashes, here standing for a grave; twain means two.
readings.contentNote: Two young officers die in a colonial war; the poem does not describe the fighting.

excerpt.locator: The Casterbridge Captains (Khyber Pass, 1842), the whole poem with its subtitle; opens “A TRADITION OF J. B. L—, T. G. B—, AND J. L—.”; closes “…longer lit his brain; Transcendence rayed the distant urn Where slept the fallen twain.”.

questions.prompt: What did the three do as boys, and what does the surviving captain find when he comes home?
facilitatorNotes: As pupils they sat in the old church aisle and each carved his name. He finds the names still there, “of equal size,” though their fates have been unequal since: two dead, one honoured.
evidence: The names, rough-hewn, of equal size,
Stood on the panel still;

questions.prompt: “’Twas theirs to aim, / Mine was it to fulfil!” What does he mean? Does it sound like a boast or like grief?
facilitatorNotes: They aimed at glory; he lived to achieve it, and wears “The laurels all had earned.” It could be proud (he alone completed the task) or humble (he finished what they began, so the honour is theirs too).
evidence: The laurels all had earned.
Mine was it to fulfil!

questions.prompt: Why does the preacher’s text, “Who saves his life shall lose it,” strike him, though the preacher does not know he is there?
facilitatorNotes: It is a saying of Jesus. The survivor has, literally, saved his life; the words suggest he may have lost something the dead have kept. The coincidence turns an ordinary sermon into a judgment, and he looks at the names again.
evidence: Unweeting he his listener, who
Looked at the names again.

questions.prompt: By the end, who has the “Transcendent triumph”? Do you agree with the captain’s change of mind?
facilitatorNotes: He sees that only “the chance of war” divided them, and that death gave the others a “majesty / Which living failed to give”; his own triumph no longer lights his mind. Some readers agree that sacrifice ennobles; others hear survivor’s guilt, or a poem quietly questioning how the dead are glorified.
evidence: ’Twas but the chance of war:
Transcendence rayed the distant urn

readings.title: To Outer Nature
readings.challenge: Unpack a very short poem of rare words and quick rhymes, and hear the sadness under its light sound.
readings.focus: Growing up as losing a belief that the world was made to delight us.
readings.context: Thomas Hardy (1840–1928), best known for his novels of rural Wessex, his name for southwest England, published his first book of poems, Wessex Poems, in 1898; it gathers verse written over thirty years, some of it in the 1860s. Outer Nature is the natural world outside the mind. Hardy packs this poem with unusual words: “omen-scouting” means looking for signs; to expound is to explain; an endowment is a gift; “irisèd” means rainbow-coloured, after Iris, the Greek goddess of the rainbow; an embowment is an arch, like a bower; meetness is fitness or rightness; sempiternal means everlasting; vernal means of spring; hodiernal means of today. The short lines rhyme in pairs, many with two-syllable rhymes.

excerpt.locator: To Outer Nature, the whole poem; opens “SHOW thee as I thought thee When I early sought thee, Omen-scouting, All undoubting Love…”; closes “…Thou and I? Our vernal Brightness keeping, Time outleaping; Passed the hodiernal!”.

questions.prompt: What did the speaker once believe about nature, according to the first two stanzas?
facilitatorNotes: When young, “All undoubting,” he believed love alone had made nature, for his pleasure, as a way of “expounding / And resounding / Glad things”: a world designed to be kind and full of meaning for him.
evidence: All undoubting
Wrought thee for my pleasure,

questions.prompt: What has time done to his view? Find the lines that state the change.
facilitatorNotes: Time “forbids with scorning” any re-adorning; he sees things “Cease to be things / They were in my morning.” The change is in how he sees as much as in nature itself, and he wishes for “but a moment” of the old gift.
evidence: Time forbids with scorning—
Cease to be things They were in my morning.

questions.prompt: How do the poem’s sounds, short lines and two-syllable rhymes, fit or clash with what it says?
facilitatorNotes: The quick, songlike, almost playful sound carries a sad idea. It may echo the glad young voice the speaker has lost, so the form itself remembers his “morning”; or the cleverness may show a man keeping his grief at a distance.
evidence: When I early sought thee,
Radiance, meetness,

questions.prompt: The last stanza asks, “Why not sempiternal / Thou and I?” Is this a real question? How do you read the final line?
facilitatorNotes: He wishes that nature and he could have stayed forever young and bright, “Time outleaping.” The last line probably continues the wish, having passed beyond the merely daily, though it can also be heard as a sigh that the day is over. Either way the learned, Latin word ends the poem coolly, far from springtime.
evidence: Why not sempiternal
Passed the hodiernal!

readings.title: The Slow Nature
readings.challenge: Judge a character’s reaction to terrible news, then revise the judgment when the poem ends.
readings.focus: Quick feeling and slow feeling: how grief can be misread.
readings.context: Thomas Hardy (1840–1928), best known for his novels of rural Wessex, his name for southwest England, published his first book of poems, Wessex Poems, in 1898; it gathers verse written over thirty years, some of it in the 1860s. The subtitle calls this “An Incident of Froom Valley”: the Froom, or Frome, is the river through Hardy’s home county of Dorset, and Egdon is his name for the heath beside it. The date 1894 is printed at the end. A barton is a farmyard; a goodman is a husband; “th’lt” is “thou wilt,” you will; unwontedly means unusually; a dresser is a kitchen cupboard with shelves; sedge is a grassy plant of wet ground; a hussif is a housewife; a fortnight is two weeks; to pine is to waste away with grief.
readings.contentNote: A man is killed by a bull, and his widow dies of grief two weeks later.

excerpt.locator: The Slow Nature (An Incident of Froom Valley), the whole poem with its date; opens ““THY husband—poor, poor Heart!—is dead— Dead, out by Moreford Rise; A bull escaped the…”; closes “1894.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Mistress Damon not believe the news at first? What finally convinces her?
facilitatorNotes: Kit Twink is the village joker who has fooled her for years, so she laughs. His words do not convince her; his face does, “unwontedly sad,” and she reads the truth there.
evidence: And ever hast thou fooled me!
So unwontedly sad was the merry man’s face—

questions.prompt: What does she do in the moments after she believes it? What do the details of the stanza beginning “She laid a hand on the dresser-ledge” show?
facilitatorNotes: She steadies herself, looks far off across the heath, and stands; we hear only the wind in the sedge and the river. Hardy shows shock through stillness and the sounds outside her, not through words.
evidence: She laid a hand on the dresser-ledge,
And the rippling Froom; till she cried:

questions.prompt: Her first cry is about her unmade bed. Why might a new widow think of that? How does Kit judge it?
facilitatorNotes: Kit is “amazed” that she thinks first of her untidy room. Readers may see shock seizing on something small and manageable, or her dread of neighbours’ judgment when they carry the body up her stairs; the mind cannot yet hold the loss itself. Kit takes it for shallowness.
evidence: ‘What a slovenly hussif!’ it will be said,
Thought first of her unkempt room.

questions.prompt: What does the title mean? How does the last stanza reverse our first impressions of both characters?
facilitatorNotes: Her nature is slow: grief arrives late but goes deep, and within a fortnight she stops eating and pines away. Kit, who looked so moved, soon laughs again “in his ancient way.” The quick show of feeling was shallow; the slow one was real. Readers may debate whether Hardy blames Kit or simply observes.
evidence: But a fortnight thence she could take no food,
And laughed in his ancient way.
